newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed hints at tough talking with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed hints at tough talking with NATO.

text.p: Russia's outspoken security chief Alexander Lebed indicated that he was prepared for some blunt talking when he visited NATO headquarters on Monday during his first-ever trip to the West.
The former paratrooper and Afghan war veteran said on arrival in Brussels on Sunday that he expected a "complicated but civilised dialogue" with alliance leaders.
Lebed, 46, said he would present ideas on ending a dispute between Moscow and the 16-member alliance over its plans to expand to take in former members of the now-defunct Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.

"We will evaluate the situation from the point of view of Russia's interests and security," he said in the rumbling voice that has become familiar to Western officials since the four-star general's sudden rise to Kremlin power this year.

Lebed, former commander of Russia's 14th Army in Moldova and now President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser, once accused NATO of behaving like a "big drunken hooligan" in seeking to expand eastwards.

Lebed said he would present the proposals to NATO Secretary- General Javier Solana. He also said his visit was closely co-ordinated with the Russian Foreign Ministry, which has shown some signs of softening its position on the dispute.
But it may prove difficult for alliance officials to gauge to what extent he speaks with the authority of Yeltsin, now in hospital awaiting heart surgery.

Lebed, whose paratroop units would have played a key role in any conflict between NATO and Warsaw Pact troops, would have seen the alliance for the first two decades of his career as the centre of an "imperialist" conspiracy against Communist Moscow.
Certainly he has now renounced communism as bankrupt and made vehement enemies among communist parliamentary deputies, but he still harbours misgivings about the alliance.
In an interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel, he said NATO was still prey to Cold War attitudes.

"To tell the superpower Russia that NATO's expansion process was inevitable and has nothing to do with us...I'm no diplomat but I'd advise anyone to think extremely carefully before saying something like that," he said.

Lebed has said on many occasions that he would like to succeed Yeltsin as president. Among his priorities would be increased funding for the armed forces which, he has said, are on the verge of mutiny because of unpaid wages.

As well as Solana, Lebed will meet NATO ambassadors on Monday. On Tuesday he is due to visit NATO's military command headquarters in the town of Mons, which is the centre of operations for alliance forces in Bosnia.
